key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option cut exact-minimum payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce debt, because nudged users chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum and cash-strapped users disengaged from autopay.
methodology: Randomised field experiment on live credit-card accounts, six-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Directly undermines the 'defaults always help' premise in a consumer financial product: a nominally successful nudge changed enrolment behaviour without changing the underlying outcome, exactly the 'vanity enrolment' risk support raised.
limitations: credit-card debt paydown, not savings accumulation
effect measured at 6 months only, not 12
relevance_reason: placeholder

key_finding: A synthesis of current DC plan design research covering automatic enrollment, default investments, framing effects, and their short- vs longer-term participant engagement consequences.
methodology: Narrative literature overview; abstract-only, no primary data.
why_it_matters: Gives the field-level map of what is known about default effects on engagement over time, useful as background but not a specific estimate for either the entry or level decision.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
no effect sizes given in the abstract
overview rather than primary evidence
relevance_reason: Broad state-of-the-art review of the closest analogous literature (employer DC plan defaults), useful as background context for the brief's questions.

key_finding: Default enrollment raises short-term participation but induces behavioral inertia -- low contribution rates, non-management of accounts, and account churn -- undermining long-term welfare claims based on participation alone.
methodology: Narrative policy article synthesizing prior empirical findings; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly states the internal support-team objection as a documented phenomenon: opt-out enrollment can be a 'passive trap' rather than a welfare win, which should temper the plan to default everyone in.
limitations: U.S. employer retirement system, not a consumer app
no quantitative effect sizes in the abstract
policy commentary rather than new empirical data
relevance_reason: Directly articulates and evidences the counter-argument the brief asks us to weigh against the 'defaults always help' premise.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for downstream (post-enrollment) default effects, identifying time course of choice, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators of whether default effects persist or fade.
methodology: Conceptual review and theoretical framework synthesizing prior consumer-behavior findings; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a structured way to think about exactly the question the brief raises -- whether default-driven enrollment persists or decays -- and what to measure (antecedent preference strength, trade-off salience) to predict which outcome we'll get.
limitations: conceptual/theoretical, not a specific empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
abstract gives no numeric effect sizes
relevance_reason: Consumer-behavior framework directly addressing persistence and heterogeneity of default effects, the two open empirical questions in the brief.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive to the value of the default option even when losses are substantial.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options and administrative claims data.
why_it_matters: Shows that default-driven passivity can persist even against beneficiaries' own interests, which bears directly on whether opt-out enrollees in the round-up feature would disengage rather than actively reconsider -- and that active-choice variation may be driven by transient attention rather than deliberate preference.
limitations: Medicare Part D drug plan context, not a consumer savings product
low-income beneficiary population may not generalize to app users
no financial-savings amount outcome measured
relevance_reason: Rigorous natural-experiment evidence on default persistence and the nature of active-choice variation, the closest available evidence outside pensions on how robust passivity is.

key_finding: Steady-state saving rates increase by only 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% due to default auto-escalation once job turnover, withdrawal on separation, and opt-outs are accounted for; only 40% of auto-escalation defaults escalate on the first date.
methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating employee turnover, balance withdrawal, and auto-escalation opt-out dynamics.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of our support team's objection: the enrolment lift from opt-out defaults shrinks dramatically once medium-run attrition and disengagement are modeled, directly bearing on whether an opt-out round-up default would be vanity enrollment.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated context absent from our product
auto-escalation dynamic differs from a fixed round-up multiplier
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that default enrollment reliably raises saving once medium/long-run dynamics are modeled, with numeric effect sizes.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pension system raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most affected individuals actively opted out, with default strength moderated by incentive size and knowledge of enrollment status.
methodology: Natural experiment using administrative and survey data around the nationwide introduction of auto-enrollment.
why_it_matters: A large, quantified default effect size that also shows the effect is contingent on incentive salience and awareness -- directly bears on when a round-up default would 'stick' versus be actively reversed.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension system, not a consumer app
opt-out ease and incentive structure differ from a savings feature
no data on amount saved or persistence beyond initial opt-out decision
relevance_reason: Quantified default effect size with clear moderators (incentives, knowledge), directly relevant to the entry decision even though set in a pension context.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, are substantially attenuated by 36 months, with modest average savings increases though reduced savings inequality; a life-cycle model fits this with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans and a UK representative panel, plus a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the persistence question the brief asks about (6-12+ months), showing default-driven gains fade considerably over the medium run -- evidence against assuming an opt-out default's enrollment lift translates into lasting savings gains.
limitations: retirement savings horizon (36 months) not directly comparable to a liquid round-up feature
employer-plan setting
no multiplier/level anchoring analysis
relevance_reason: Directly quantifies attenuation of default effects over time, the persistence question central to the brief, even though outside the consumer product setting.

key_finding: Defaults in wealth-management advice significantly shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default (or overriding one) lowers the client's rating of the advice received, an effect mediated by perceived advisor honesty; framing of the default question (how much to invest vs. how much to leave safe) also shifts allocations.
methodology: Three experiments including a large representative sample across five European countries (n=4207) on default and framing manipulations in investment advice.
why_it_matters: Directly tests, in an EU consumer-financial-advice setting, exactly the manipulation/reputational-risk trade-off the brief flags: a default that shifts behavior can also erode trust, and how the default and preset level are framed changes both compliance and perceived honesty -- this should shape how the round-up multiplier default is presented, not just which value is chosen.
limitations: wealth-management investment advice rather than a round-up savings feature
no persistence data beyond the experimental session
risk-taking outcome, not enrollment/contribution behavior
relevance_reason: EU consumer financial-advice experiment on defaults and framing that directly informs the manipulation/dark-pattern and anchoring questions the brief raises.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three large firms, but roughly 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default contribution rate and conservative default fund, with half still at the default rate/fund after three years, offsetting participation gains against anchoring at a low savings rate.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking automatic-enrollment participants over multiple years.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that preset levels anchor the amount people end up saving, not just whether they enroll -- the foundational result the whole default-enrollment literature, including this brief's level decision, argues from.
limitations: employer 401(k) context, decades before the app/regulatory environment described in the brief
no data on active choice or consumer fintech settings
conservative default fund choice not analogous to a round-up multiplier
relevance_reason: The foundational classic study establishing that preset default levels anchor contribution/investment choices, directly informing the level decision even though set in retirement plans.

key_finding: Default adherence in NYC taxi tipping decisions (8.6M trips) arises from friction complementarity -- 84% of adherence requires both a deviation cost and an opt-out cost simultaneously -- and adding an intermediate tip option (15%) below the existing 20/25/30% menu captures 69% of achievable welfare gains at low revenue cost.
methodology: Structural model estimated on 8.6 million tipping transactions, validated against an independent stated-preference survey.
why_it_matters: The friction-decomposition method and the menu-design finding -- that adding an intermediate preset option can recover most of the welfare benefit -- directly transfers to choosing among 1x/2x/5x round-up multiplier presets, since our multiplier menu is structurally the same kind of preset-option-with-adherence-friction problem.
limitations: tipping decisions, not financial savings behavior
single transaction decisions rather than an ongoing enrolled feature
no persistence or enrollment outcome measured
relevance_reason: Names an explicit method transfer: the friction-decomposition approach and preset-menu-option analysis apply directly to designing the round-up multiplier menu (1x/2x/5x), the brief's level decision.

key_finding: In an opt-in short-term savings program at five U.K. firms, take-up was extremely low (no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account), but among those who did opt in, 96% still held a positive balance and 87% received a payroll contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of program introduction and administrative account data tracked over 12 months at five U.K. firms.
why_it_matters: This is the closest prior work to our exact product: a liquid, withdrawable, payroll-linked savings account under opt-in enrollment. It shows opt-in alone yields near-vanishing scale despite strong retention among enrollees -- direct evidence for the entry-design trade-off between enrollment scale (opt-out/active choice) and engagement quality (opt-in) that the brief is deciding.
limitations: enrollment is via employer payroll deduction, not a self-service app, so the channel-to-attention differs
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice conditions in this sample
UK employer context rather than EU consumer app
relevance_reason: Closest prior work on a liquid, short-term, opt-in savings product, directly quantifying the take-up vs. retention trade-off central to the entry-design decision; the product studied (payroll-linked short-term savings) is far closer to a round-up feature than any retirement plan.

key_finding: Characterizes optimal default options analytically: when the designer and choosers agree on the activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions to Pigouvian fees and cases of designer-chooser disagreement.
methodology: Theoretical/asymptotic analysis with numerical simulations validating approximation accuracy; abstract-only beyond that.
why_it_matters: Offers a normative framework for choosing which default level (e.g. which multiplier to preset) minimizes welfare loss under agreement vs. disagreement about the 'right' saving amount, informing how to reason about the level decision beyond pure empirics.
limitations: purely theoretical, no empirical validation in a financial-product setting
abstract gives no applied numbers or population
assumes designer/chooser value structure that may not map cleanly onto round-up savings
relevance_reason: General optimal-default theory offering a normative lens for the level-preset decision, though it requires translation from abstract theory to the specific product.

key_finding: Maps EU dark-pattern law onto a six-category autonomy-violation taxonomy, showing the regulation targets exploitation of consumer biases rather than banning defaults or pre-selection outright.
methodology: Legal-doctrinal analysis and taxonomy construction; abstract-only, no empirical data.
why_it_matters: Gives the specific EU legal test for when an opt-out default becomes a dark pattern, directly bounding how the enrolment default and disclosure can be designed without reputational or legal risk.
limitations: legal/doctrinal analysis, not empirical evidence on enrolment or savings outcomes
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: Directly informs the EU dark-pattern/manipulation-risk question the brief flags as a reputational constraint on the opt-out design.

key_finding: A 12% default contribution rate left 25% of employees still at that (likely suboptimal) default after 12 months, versus roughly half remaining at lower defaults in the prior literature.
methodology: Administrative data from an employer retirement plan with a high default, benchmarked against a literature review of lower-default plans.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether a high preset level anchors people who would otherwise choose differently, informing which round-up multiplier to preselect and how strongly it will stick.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
no discussion of how the employer-intermediary mechanism differs from a self-directed app
relevance_reason: Closest available high-quality evidence on whether a preset contribution level anchors the eventual chosen level, the exact mechanism behind the round-up multiplier decision.

key_finding: Abstract text was not retrievable ('Trant'); the title indicates four large UK field experiments automating short-term payroll savings.
methodology: abstract-only 	itle..no title and metadata are usable.
why_it_matters: Potentially the closest analogue to round-up savings (short-term, liquid, automated) from a research group behind related papers in this set, but the missing abstract leaves no usable evidence for the decision.
limitations: abstract not available, so no effect sizes or design details can be assessed
payroll savings are still routed through an employer, unlike a standalone banking app
relevance_reason: Title suggests direct relevance to short-term automated savings design, but the abstract provides no extractable evidence.

key_finding: At-scale automatic enrolment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts at UK banks cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million market-wide.
methodology: Large-scale field experiments run directly inside UK bank consumer accounts.
why_it_matters: The closest real-world precedent for auto-enrolling consumers into a banking-app feature by default rather than by choice, in the same consumer-financial, self-directed setting as the round-up feature - evidence that opt-out defaults inside a bank app can produce real financial benefit, not just nominal sign-up.
limitations: measures downstream financial outcomes (overdraft charges) rather than enrolment or contribution-level persistence directly
no comparison against opt-in or active-choice enrolment
relevance_reason: Directly analogous consumer-banking automatic-enrolment field experiment, the nearest real-world precedent to the round-up feature itself.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrolment raised savings by roughly £32-38/month but this was partly offset by about £7/month more unsecured debt and higher mortgage balances over 41 months, though defaults also lowered defaults on loans and raised credit scores.
methodology: Large-scale natural experiment from the UK automatic-enrolment pension roll-out to ~160,000 small employers.
why_it_matters: Directly challenges the assumption that a default-driven rise in nominal savings represents a clean gain - some of the 'saved' money is financed by more borrowing, exactly the kind of net-effect question behind the support team's 'vanity number' objection.
limitations: employer-mediated pension context, not a self-directed consumer banking app
debt-offset mechanism may not generalize to small, liquid round-up sums
relevance_reason: Best available large-scale evidence that a default-driven rise in nominal savings can be substantially offset elsewhere in the household balance sheet, directly bearing on whether the enrolment number is meaningful.

key_finding: Removing an auto-enrolment default and adding one extra enrolment step cut health-insurance enrolment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment studying removal of an auto-enrolment policy in a public health-insurance program, with a selection-market model.
why_it_matters: Shows that adding friction to enrolment (comparable to choosing opt-in over opt-out) does not selectively screen out low-value users - it disproportionately excludes vulnerable groups, a direct warning about who gets hurt if we rely on friction to filter enrolment.
limitations: health-insurance selection market, not a consumer savings product
the friction mechanism (ordeal) differs from a simple opt-in/opt-out toggle
relevance_reason: Strong quantified evidence on how enrolment friction differentially harms disadvantaged groups, bearing directly on the brief's distributional, who's-hurt question.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults raised donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with larger effects on smaller and less-experienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across political campaign websites around the 2020 US election.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can move nominal financial commitment (recurring donations) without users intending it, evidenced by elevated refund requests - precisely the 'passively enrolled, didn't understand what they signed up for' failure mode the support team worries about for round-up enrolment.
limitations: political donations, not a savings product
US election context, not the EU consumer-protection regulatory setting
relevance_reason: The clearest empirical demonstration that a recurring-financial-commitment default can produce unintended, regretted enrolment, direct evidence for the manipulation/dark-pattern risk the brief flags.

key_finding: In a search model with a default option, the default raises the reservation utility (reference effect) and induces self-selection into search by those most likely to find a better option, both confirmed experimentally.
methodology: Lab experiments testing a theoretical reference-dependent search model.
why_it_matters: Offers a theoretical mechanism for why defaults might not simply anchor people passively - some fraction actively search past the default - relevant background for predicting whether users would deviate from a preset multiplier.
limitations: abstract general-choice lab experiment, not a financial or savings product
no measure of enrolment persistence or amount saved
relevance_reason: General theoretical evidence on the mechanism behind default anchoring in search/choice, tangential background for the multiplier-preset question.

key_finding: After the EU Digital Markets Act mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects observed from 15 months after rollout onward.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design around the staggered rollout of DMA-mandated choice screens on iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: Directly answers whether forced active choice can meaningfully shift outcomes away from an incumbent default in a mobile-app, EU-regulatory setting nearly identical to ours, evidence that active choice's effect persists well past onboarding.
limitations: outcome is browser usage, not financial enrolment or savings amount
platform-level natural experiment, not a within-app active-choice test
relevance_reason: The closest available natural experiment on active choice versus default in an EU-regulated mobile-app setting, directly bearing on the active-choice-vs-default decision.

key_finding: Among nine opt-out interface designs tested with 410 participants, generalizable schemes sharply reduced opt-out disruption (98% felt undisrupted for the best scheme, a 40-point improvement) while only slightly reducing opt-out utility.
methodology: Usability study comparing nine privacy-choice interface schemes implemented in a browser extension, n=410.
why_it_matters: Provides a template for designing an active-choice or opt-out interface that is legally compliant (no default-on) and low-friction, informing how a forced-choice onboarding screen for round-up could be built without frustrating users.
limitations: domain is privacy consent (GPC), not financial savings enrolment
usability outcomes measured, not actual financial behaviour or persistence
relevance_reason: Closest available empirical work on designing low-disruption non-default (active) choice interfaces, relevant to building an active-choice onboarding screen without harming completion.

key_finding: Opt-out defaults increased sign-up in both single-exam and many-exam settings, but only translated into greater effortful task completion (participation and passing) for the single, strongly-endorsed default and only among previously responsive individuals; for many exams and non-responsive individuals there was no effect on actual outcomes despite higher sign-up.
methodology: Two field experiments changing university exam sign-up to opt-out, tracking downstream effortful outcomes (participation, passing).
why_it_matters: The most direct evidence available that a default can raise nominal enrolment without increasing the effortful behaviour it's meant to produce unless targeted at people already inclined to engage, exactly the 'passively enrolled users don't engage' concern the support team raises about round-up savings.
limitations: university exam sign-up, not a financial savings product
effort/engagement measured through exam behaviour, not money saved or withdrawn
relevance_reason: Directly tests whether an opt-out default that raises sign-up also raises real engagement, the core mechanism behind the brief's disengagement worry, making it the closest available evidence on that specific question despite the non-financial setting.

key_finding: After a law let target-date funds become default investments, younger workers' default-driven stock allocation rose and older workers' fell in line with the default glidepath, but contribution rates barely changed.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of US middle-class investors, 2006-2018, exploiting the Pension Protection Act default-option change.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can strongly anchor an allocation choice while leaving the separate contribution-rate decision almost untouched, a caution that a preset round-up multiplier might anchor the multiplier choice without moving how much people actually save overall.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement investment defaults, not a consumer savings-amount decision
measures portfolio allocation, not enrolment or withdrawal behaviour
relevance_reason: Evidence that default effects can be strong on one dimension (allocation) and negligible on another (contribution rate), relevant to whether presetting the multiplier would move total amounts saved.

key_finding: In an RCT of 220 participants, social-norm, framing, default-option, and positive-narrative nudges all significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings relative to control, contrary to prevailing international evidence, with the largest backfire from positive-narrative and default-option nudges.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey, 220 participants, testing multiple behavioural nudges including default options on voluntary pension contributions.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the brief's working assumption that 'defaults will lift enrolment' - here the default nudge backfired and reduced willingness to contribute, with heterogeneity by income, education, gender, and trust, underscoring that context and institutional trust determine whether a default helps or hurts.
limitations: small online-survey sample (n=220) in China, cultural/institutional context differs from the EU
voluntary pension framing rather than a bank-app round-up feature
relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in the set: an RCT where default options actively reduced willingness to save, directly undercutting the premise the brief asks us to test.

key_finding: A representative Australian sample (n=2,100) rated financial nudges positively overall, favoured System-2 (reflective) interventions and savings-framed messaging, and did not find transparency to reduce approval, though manipulation perceptions varied by framing.
methodology: Pre-registered survey experiment with 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios varying transparency, framing, and System-1/System-2 targeting; six outcome measures including manipulation and likelihood of bank use.
why_it_matters: Directly tests when a bank-proposed financial default or nudge is perceived as manipulative versus helpful, which is the exact reputational question the EU dark-pattern concern raises for choosing opt-out entry.
limitations: hypothetical scenarios rather than actual product use
Australian sample, not EU
no measurement of actual enrolment or savings behaviour
relevance_reason: Provides direct consumer-facing evidence on manipulation/approval perceptions of financial defaults, the missing piece for the dark-pattern risk question.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries a bank-account payment option had no significant average effect on savings, but raised balances for those who previously had nonpositive balances.
methodology: Field experiment with conditional cash transfer beneficiaries comparing cash vs. bank-account delivery, abstract-only detail.
why_it_matters: Suggests defaulting people into savings accounts mainly helps those starting from zero, a distributional pattern relevant to who benefits from auto-enrolment, but the setting (subsidy delivery to low-income beneficiaries) is far from a consumer banking app.
limitations: developing-country cash-transfer population, not a fintech consumer app
measures account balances not round-up-style contributions
no data on persistence beyond study window
relevance_reason: Offers a heterogeneity finding (defaults help nonsavers more) analogous to the distributional question in C5, though setting is distant.

key_finding: Compares outcomes of a universal automatic IRA design with an attached emergency (liquid) savings component against alternatives with identical contribution levels.
methodology: Abstract-only; appears to be a policy-design comparison of automatic enrolment structures including a liquid emergency-savings feature.
why_it_matters: A liquid emergency-savings sidecar attached to an automatic-enrolment retirement vehicle is structurally close to a round-up feature with an exit option, informing whether persistent liquid balances survive automatic enrolment.
limitations: abstract is a truncated fragment, so key findings and effect sizes are not extractable
policy-level design analysis rather than individual behavioural data
not a bank fintech product
relevance_reason: Closest available analogue combining automatic enrolment with a liquid savings component, bearing on persistence of liquid balances under defaults.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrolment dramatically raised participation, and most auto-enrolled employees stuck to both the default contribution rate and default fund allocation.
methodology: Before/after natural experiment using administrative payroll and plan data from one large US corporation around a 401(k) design change.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that default enrolment status and default contribution level both anchor behaviour strongly; the literature this project's default-effect and anchoring questions ultimately trace back to.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan with employer as trusted intermediary, the mechanism the brief says does not transfer
locked, illiquid savings vehicle unlike a round-up feature
2001 data predates app-based consumer finance and current EU regulatory climate
relevance_reason: Closest foundational prior work establishing both the default-enrolment effect and anchoring on preset contribution levels that the brief's C1/C3 questions are built on.

key_finding: Compares savings behaviours of employees under automatic versus voluntary enrolment in a defined-contribution retirement plan.
methodology: Abstract not provided; presumed comparative observational analysis of plan participants under the two enrolment regimes.
why_it_matters: Another data point on auto- vs voluntary-enrolment savings behaviour, but with no abstract content to assess effect size, depth, or mechanism relevant to the build decision.
limitations: no abstract available to verify findings or methodology
employer-sponsored retirement plan setting
forthcoming/unpublished (2026), unverified
relevance_reason: Topically on-point comparison of enrolment regimes but too little information to move the decision.

key_finding: Institutional mistrust and minority/non-national status were significantly associated with both under-saving and early withdrawal from a previously mandatory pension scheme after a policy reform allowed withdrawal.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around an early-withdrawal pension reform.
why_it_matters: Directly speaks to the support team's fear that passively-enrolled or low-trust users disengage and withdraw quickly, and identifies which subgroups are most likely to be harmed by an opt-out design.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme, not a self-directed consumer fintech product
Estonian institutional-trust context may not generalise to an EU banking-app population
withdrawal is a policy-reform event, not routine liquid access
relevance_reason: Gives a distributional/persistence account of who disengages and withdraws, matching the brief's C2/C5 concerns about vanity enrolment and harm to vulnerable users.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, reflecting on a hypothetical default (automatic) vaccination-booster enrolment policy reduced stated vaccination intentions and policy approval rather than increasing them.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries manipulating reflection on a hypothetical default-enrolment policy.
why_it_matters: Shows that when people are prompted to notice a default, it can backfire and reduce both stated behaviour and approval — direct evidence against the premise that defaults always help, relevant to how an opt-out round-up feature might read once users notice it.
limitations: health/vaccination policy domain, not a financial product
hypothetical policy scenario, not observed behaviour
no financial or savings context
relevance_reason: Contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise by showing reflection on a default can produce backlash, directly bearing on the EU dark-pattern/manipulation-perception risk named in the brief.

key_finding: Automatic enrolment and employer contribution provisions were associated with higher retirement-plan participation among US Millennials in 2018 FINRA survey data.
methodology: Cross-sectional survey analysis (2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study) controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance, and assets.
why_it_matters: Replicates the well-established auto-enrolment participation lift in a newer cohort, but adds little beyond confirming an already-settled finding for an employer-plan context.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans with employer-matching, the intermediary mechanism the brief excludes
cross-sectional survey, no persistence or withdrawal data
not a liquid consumer savings product
relevance_reason: Confirms the default-enrolment effect size in a modern cohort but does not extend beyond what is already assumed in the brief.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic (passive) employer contributions raised wealth accumulation substantially, while active-choice tax subsidies induced only $0.01 of extra saving per $1 of subsidy because 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but heavily moved by automatic defaults.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis of Danish retirement savings responses to active-choice subsidies versus passive/automatic contribution policies.
why_it_matters: The most rigorous large-sample evidence distinguishing active-choice from passive-default savings responses and quantifying who is a 'passive' versus 'active' saver — the clearest large-scale precedent for the active-choice-vs-default comparison in C6, even though the intermediary is an employer.
limitations: automatic employer contributions, not consumer self-enrolment in a savings app
Danish tax-advantaged retirement accounts, illiquid relative to a round-up feature
active vs passive savers defined by tax-subsidy response, not exactly enrolment default
relevance_reason: Closest large-sample evidence on active-choice versus passive-default savings responses and the heterogeneity between active and passive savers, foundational to the C6 active-choice question despite the employer setting.

key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' (forcing a yes/no decision with no default) can be strengthened into 'enhanced active choice,' which highlights losses from the non-preferred option, as an alternative to automatic enrolment when opt-out is infeasible or ethically fraught.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and a novel enhanced active-choice variant against no-default and default conditions.
why_it_matters: Supplies the specific mechanism (forced choice plus loss-framed messaging) that the brief's decision 1 is directly choosing between opt-in/opt-out/active choice — a concrete design for capturing enrolment benefit without full auto-enrolment.
limitations: medication-adherence and general behaviour-change settings, not a financial product
no financial-savings outcome measured
field experiments are the studies reviewed rather than a single large trial with a stated effect size
relevance_reason: Explicit method transfer: the active-choice and enhanced-active-choice design tested here is precisely the third entry-design option the brief must decide between, and the loss-framing technique for the non-default option carries directly into UI copy design.

key_finding: A synthesis of household-finance research covering consumption/savings, choice architecture, product design, and defaults as one of several intervention classes shaping household financial behaviour.
methodology: Narrative review/chapter summarising empirical regularities and behavioural interventions across household finance topics; abstract-only detail here.
why_it_matters: Gives the project a synthesis-level view of where defaults and choice architecture sit among other consumer-finance interventions (education, disclosure, product design), useful for weighing default design against non-default levers.
limitations: broad chapter covering many topics, not focused specifically on enrolment defaults for liquid savings
abstract gives no effect sizes
mixes employer-plan and consumer-finance literatures without separating the intermediary distinction the brief flags
relevance_reason: The review/meta-level synthesis the brief asks for, situating default and choice-architecture effects within the broader household-finance intervention literature.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrolment raised participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and default conservative fund, with half still anchored on the default after three years.
methodology: Multi-year administrative data analysis from three large US firms comparing automatic versus voluntary 401(k) enrolment.
why_it_matters: Closest prior work directly quantifying anchoring on a preset default contribution level and its persistence over years, the exact evidence needed for the C3 decision on whether to pre-set a round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) plan with employer as trusted intermediary, the mechanism the brief says does not carry over
illiquid long-horizon retirement savings versus liquid round-up sweeps
2001 data predates app-based fintech and current EU regulatory norms
relevance_reason: Closest prior work quantifying both the default-enrolment effect and, specifically, anchoring at a preset contribution level over multiple years — directly informing the multiplier pre-set decision.

key_finding: Randomly assigning employees to default enrolment in a salary-linked savings account increased participation by 40 percentage points, an effect equivalent to a 50% matching incentive, driven mainly by present bias and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among Afghan employees testing several salary-linked savings account default variants and follow-up interventions to isolate mechanisms.
why_it_matters: Identifies the psychological mechanism behind default effects (cognitive cost, present bias), useful for predicting whether a round-up default will produce durable behaviour change or just passive inertia, and suggests active decisions can persist after default assignment ends.
limitations: salary-linked account for employees, an employer-adjacent payment channel not a consumer banking app
different economic and cultural context (Afghanistan) from an EU fintech user base
no data on withdrawal or disengagement over 6-12 months
relevance_reason: Provides rigorous causal estimate and mechanism for the default effect size (C1) and touches on why defaults may or may not produce lasting engagement, relevant by close analogy despite the employer-linked setting.

key_finding: A field-experiment reminder nudge cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial-management platform in Brazil; abstract-only for further design detail.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the brief's central worry — a well-intentioned nudge can help most users on average while making a vulnerable subgroup worse off — which should push the team toward monitoring distributional outcomes (e.g. overdraft-prone users) before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: studies reminder nudges, not enrollment defaults, so it does not directly measure opt-in/opt-out/active-choice effects
credit-card and overdraft context rather than a savings round-up product
abstract gives no long-horizon (6-12 month) persistence data
relevance_reason: Provides the strongest available consumer-finance evidence on heterogeneous, sometimes harmful, side effects of a well-meaning nudge — exactly the distributional risk (C5) the brief flags as a reason not to default everyone in.
